primary_claim: Prompt injection succeeds because LLMs infer a token's role (e.g. <user> vs <tool>) from surface writing style rather than its actual role tag; role probes show spoofed reasoning tokens register the same high 'CoTness' as genuine <think> tokens even when stripped of tags or wrapped in <user> tags, and exploiting this with a new attack (CoT Forgery) raises jailbreak attack success rates from near-zero to ~60%, generalizing across every LLM tested.

effect.metric: jailbreak attack success rate with CoT Forgery vs baseline
effect.value: near-zero to ~60% (destyling the spoofed reasoning drops it from 61% to 10%)

contradicts_or_qualifies: standard prompt injection benchmarks show near-perfect model scores, but human red-teamers achieve near-100% attack success rates against the same frontier models, indicating benchmark scores reflect attack memorization rather than genuine robustness
stated_future_work: study 'subconscious steering': how seemingly innocuous text (e.g. tone of a webpage) could subtly shift an LLM's state toward an intended goal, legally and at scale
explore what other objective conflicts suggest new roles, e.g. a dedicated planning role so agents treat plans as commitments, or a dedicated eval role to reduce sycophancy
study whether <user>-token activations (loss-masked, comprehension-only) could be a clean window into what the model actually understands, unpolluted by the generation signal
study what information is lost or suppressed between late <think> tokens and early <assistant> tokens to understand how LLMs verbalize computation
investigate whether roles could be dynamic, introduced at inference time, and whether models can learn role separation as a meta-skill
quote: On a standard jailbreak benchmark, CoT Forgery takes attack success rates from near-zero to ~60%, and it generalized across every LLM we tested.
